<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>—an open, light-weight moderation tool for LLM safety that achieves three goals: (1) identifying malicious intent in user prompts, (2) detecting safety risks of model responses, and (3) determining model refusal rate. Together, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> serves the increasing needs for automatic safety moderation and evaluation of LLM interactions, providing a one-stop tool with enhanced accuracy and broad coverage across 13 risk categories. While existing open moderation tools such as Llama-Guard2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> score reasonably well in classifying straightforward model interactions, they lag far behind a prompted GPT-4, especially in identifying adversarial jailbreaks and in evaluating models’ refusals, a key measure for evaluating safety behaviors in model responses.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we construct <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span>, a large-scale and carefully balanced multi-task safety moderation dataset with 92K labeled examples that cover vanilla (direct) prompts and adversarial jailbreaks, paired with various refusal and compliance responses. <span id="abstract1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span> is a combination of <span id="abstract1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span>, the training data of <span id="abstract1.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, and <span id="abstract1.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span>, a high-quality human-annotated moderation test set with 5K labeled items covering broad risk scenarios.
Through extensive evaluations on <span id="abstract1.2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span> and ten existing public benchmarks, we show that <span id="abstract1.2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> establishes state-of-the-art performance in open-source safety moderation across all the three tasks compared to ten strong existing open-source moderation models (e.g., up to 26.4% improvement on refusal detection). Importantly, <span id="abstract1.2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> matches and sometimes exceeds GPT-4 performance (e.g., up to 3.9% improvement on prompt harmfulness identification). <span id="abstract1.2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> serves as a highly effective safety moderator in an LLM interface, reducing the success rate of jailbreak attacks from 79.8% to 2.4%.</p>
    
<table id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="abstract1.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="abstract1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><img src="2406.18495v1/figures/github.png" id="abstract1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:15/15;" width="15" height="15" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> <span id="abstract1.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model</span>: <a href="https://github.com/allenai/wildguard" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/allenai/wildguard</a></td></tr>
<tr id="abstract1.3.2" class="ltx_tr">

</table>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Systems using modern Language Models (LMs) pose considerable risks if not adequately safeguarded 
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Effective content moderation is essential to mitigating these risks by filtering out undesired inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, monitoring harmful model completions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, and evaluating effectiveness of model safeguards by measuring refusal rates on harmful versus benign prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, a light-weight, multi-purpose moderation tool for assessing the safety of user-LLM interactions. <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> provides a one-stop resource for three safety moderation tasks: detection of prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness, and response refusal.
We show that <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> advances the state-of-the art of open-source safety moderation tools across all three tasks and provides a more open, consistent, and economical alternative to costly and non-static API moderation tools, achieving on-par or better performance relative to the GPT-4 judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The development of <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> is motivated in particular by two observations.
First, existing open tools like Llama-Guard2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> are much less effective for discerning harm in <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">adversarial</em> prompts (i.e., jailbreaks) compared to vanilla (i.e., direct) queries, and fall far behind GPT-4 on both.
Second, while existing open tools can to an extent identify harm in responses, the <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">harmfulness</em> of a response is insufficient to determine whether a model <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refuses</em> to answer a user’s prompt.
This is critical, for instance, for testing exaggerated safety: if a user asks “How to kill a Python process?”, responses are typically benign regardless of over-refusal (“I can’t provide instructions for acts of violence”) or correct compliance (“The way to kill a Python process is…”).
Thus, classifying harm is not sufficient for evaluating safety, making independent assessment of refusal necessary.
Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that most existing moderation models do not consider this task separately—and the single model that does performs poorly compared to GPT-4 (§<a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2406.18495v1/WildGuard_fig_v6.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/252;" width="476" height="252" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>(Top) Breakdown of <span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span>, featuring four data types: Synthetic Vanilla/Adversarial, <span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span>, and Annotator-written data. Synthetic data is a balanced mix of benign/harmful prompts, paired with compliances and refusals to each prompt, covering wide risk categories. (Bottom) Examples in <span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span>. </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these gaps, we construct <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span>, a carefully balanced, multi-task moderation dataset with 92K labeled examples covering 13 risk categories, constituting the largest multi-task safety dataset to date. Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows an overview of the data composition and examples. Data are drawn from four sources (see §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 WildGuardTrain: Multi-task Moderation Training Dataset ‣ 3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>)
to maximize coverage, with a careful balance of prompt harmfulness, vanilla vs. adversarial structure, and pairing of refusals and compliances across prompts.
<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span> consists of <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span>, the training data of <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> with 87K examples, and <span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span>, a high-quality moderation evaluation data with 5,299 human-annotated items for the three tasks (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 WildGuardTest: A High-Quality Human-Annotated Test Moderation Dataset ‣ 3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our comprehensive evaluations on <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span> and ten existing public benchmarks show that <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms the strongest existing open-source baselines (e.g., Llama-Guard2, Aegis-Guard, etc) on F1 scores across all three tasks (by up to 26.4% on refusal detection), matches GPT-4 across tasks, and surpasses GPT-4 by up to 3.9% on adversarial prompt harmfulness (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Through systematic ablations, we show that each component in <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span> is critical to the success of <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, and multi-task training improves the performance of <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> compared to single-task safeguards (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 WildGuard Ablation Results ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>). Finally, we show that <span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> can be used as a moderator on human-LLM interactions, reducing success rate on jailbreak attacks from 79.8% to 2.4% with <span id="S1.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> in the interface, without over-refusing benign user requests (§<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Demonstrating WildGuard as a Moderator in Human-LLM Interactions ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>

<td id="S2.T1.4.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T1.4.11.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>

<td id="S2.T1.4.11.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T1.4.11.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.11.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T1.4.11.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#CC4D4D;">✗</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.11.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T1.4.11.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#CC4D4D;">✗</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.4.12" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.12.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.4.12.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#4DCC4D;">✓</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first examine the current state-of-the-art moderation tools for our three tasks, and we identify several key limitations that motivate our development of <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We highlight existing classification performance in two areas: 1) <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">detecting harmfulness of adversarial prompts</span>, and 2) <span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">detecting nuanced refusal/compliance in completions</span>.
The first focus is motivated by our observation that adversarial user prompts are common in in-the-wild interactions, but they present a unique challenge for harm detection. Our second focus is motivated by the fact that tests of exaggerated safety, as in XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>,
also present a labeling challenge, being poorly-served by response harm (as we lay out in the introduction), and often eliciting especially complex responses—but still critically requiring accurate labeling for reliable evaluation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test Benchmarks</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate harm detection in adversarial prompts, we sample a uniform mixture of 250 benign and 250 harmful prompts from the validation set of <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildJailbreak</span> (<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WJ</span>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>,
a large-scale dataset consisting of adversarial and vanilla queries from diverse harm categories.
To evaluate nuanced refusal detection, we use our novel benchmark <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span>, which we describe in §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 WildGuardTest: A High-Quality Human-Annotated Test Moderation Dataset ‣ 3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. For comparison, we also show results on our third task, response harmfulness, on <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate both open-source and closed tools on these tests. Among open-source tools we test four models instruction-tuned to identify harmfulness in both prompts and responses: Llama-Guard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, Llama-Guard2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, Aegis-Guard-Defensive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, and Aegis-Guard-Permissive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
For these models, to label refusal we mark a response as compliance if the output is harmful, and as a refusal if the output label is safe. We show results for harmful prompts only (RR(h) in Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Models ‣ 2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), as this mapping is more likely to succeed in this setting.
We also test LibrAI-LongFormer-ref,
which is trained to detect refusals on the Do-Not-Answer benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> and used for evaluations in TrustLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>. Lastly, we test a keyword-based classifier, which identifies refusals using a predefined list of refusal keywords (see our list of keywords in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Keyword-based Refusal Detection ‣ Appendix F Additional Details about Existing Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>). We evaluate the latter two models only on refusal detection. We also assess two API-based tools: GPT-4 <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            We use <span id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4-0125-preview</span> for all our experiments.</span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> and OpenAI Moderation API <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. For GPT-4 we experiment with various prompts and select the one that results in best performance. We provide this prompt in Table <a href="#A6.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ F.2 GPT-4 Classification ‣ Appendix F Additional Details about Existing Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> of Appendix <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 GPT-4 Classification ‣ Appendix F Additional Details about Existing Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>. OpenAI Moderation API returns labels for toxicity, which we use for prompt and response harmfulness.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.fig3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Finding 1: Existing open tools are unreliable on adversarial prompts and far behind GPT-4.</span>
We see in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Models ‣ 2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> that existing open tools perform decently in detecting harm in vanilla prompts, but struggle to do so in adversarial prompts. For both prompt types we also see a sizeable performance gap for open tools relative to GPT-4, thus perpetuating costly reliance on API tools.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Finding 2: Existing open tools struggle with measuring refusals in model responses.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Models ‣ 2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that open tools also struggle to identify refusals in models’ completions. The top-performing harm-detection model, Llama-Guard2,
trails GPT-4 by 15.1%, validating that response harmfulness is inadequate for this task—but even
LibrAI-LongFormer-ref, a model trained specifically for refusal detection, only modestly outperforms the simple keyword-based baseline, and trails GPT-4 by 24.3%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, these patterns show non-trivial room for improvement in existing open-source tools, and a collection of related needs that can be filled by a high-quality multi-purpose moderation classifier.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Building <span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span> and <span id="S3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the insights from §<a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and by a lack of transparency in training of existing moderation tools,
we develop two datasets, <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span> and <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span> as part of <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span>. Here we describe how we curate these datasets, and how we train <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span><span id="S3.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span>: Multi-task Moderation Training Dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span> (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span>) is a comprehensive training dataset of total 86,759 items, composed of data from diverse sources and amounting to 48,783 standalone prompts + 37,976 prompt-response pairs. The dataset covers both vanilla (direct request)
and adversarial prompts across benign and harmful scenarios, as well as diverse types of refusals and compliances. <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span> includes four sources of data—synthetic adversarial, synthetic vanilla, real-world user-LLM interactions (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span>),
and existing annotator-written data—
all selected to optimize coverage, diversity, and balance for our three tasks. Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> provides an overview of the dataset composition.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Prompt Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vanilla harmful synthetic prompts.</span>
We synthetically generate
harmful prompts covering a broad range of risk scenarios. Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weidinger et al. [37]</a></cite>, we consider 13 harm subcategories
in four high-level categories: <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">privacy</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">misinformation</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">harmful language</span>, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">malicious uses</span>. Table <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ C.6 Fine-grained Risk Taxonomy of WildGuardMix ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS6" title="C.6 Fine-grained Risk Taxonomy of WildGuardMix ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.6</span></a> lists harm categories with statistics of our data. To generate targeted, realistic, and diverse harmful scenarios, we design a structured generation pipeline, detailed in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 A Pipeline for Vanilla Harmful Synthetic Prompts ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vanilla benign synthetic prompts.</span>
Similarly to <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildJailbreak</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, to enable maximally precise detection of prompt harmfulness,
we additionally include two types of benign contrastive prompts: 1) benign prompts that superficially resemble unsafe prompts, motivated by the 10 exaggerated categories<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              Homonyms, figurative language, safe targets, safe contexts, definitions, real discrimination/nonsense group, nonsense discrimination/real group, historical events, public privacy, and fictional privacy.</span></span></span> from XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, and 2) benign prompts discussing sensitive but safe topics. These vanilla benign contrastive prompts are generated with GPT-4. Refer to Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ C.3 Examples for Vanilla Benign Prompts ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 GPT-4 Instructions for Generating Vanilla Prompts ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a> for the GPT-4 prompt used to generate the queries and to Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ C.3 Examples for Vanilla Benign Prompts ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> for examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial benign and harmful synthetic prompts.</span>
We employ the <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildTeaming</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> framework to convert our generated vanilla prompts—harmful and benign—to adversarial prompts. This framework mines jailbreaking tactics
from in-the-wild user-LLM interactions, and composes selections of tactics to transform vanilla requests into diverse adversarial counterparts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompts from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span> and existing annotator-written data.</span>
We consider two types of public data: 1) in-the-wild data that we label for harmfulness and 2) existing annotator-written safety data.
To cover harm risks in real-world user requests, we include prompts
from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LMSYS-Chat-1M</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildChat</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> datasets, both of which capture in-the-wild human-LLM interactions, with harm labels assigned based on the OpenAI Moderation API.
Additionally we add subsamples of existing annotator-written safety datasets to further enhance coverage. This includes
prompts from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HH-RLHF</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> and the Anthropic Red-Teaming dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, including the subsets that make up AegisSafetyTrain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Safety-Tuned Llamas</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Compliance and Refusal Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM response generations.</span> For our synthetic adversarial and vanilla prompts, we generate matched refusal and compliance responses. We submit each prompt to a suite of LLMs,<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              OLMo-7B-Instruct, GPT-3.5, Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Llama3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, and Dolphin variants of <span id="footnote3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dolphin-2.9.1-llama-3-8b</span>, <span id="footnote3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dolphin-2.8-gemma-7b</span>, and <span id="footnote3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dolphin-2.8-mistral-7b-v02</span>.</span></span></span> along with a prompt suffix instructing the LLM to refuse or to comply with the prompt. This provides us with a set of refusal and compliance candidates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 complex response generations.</span> We additionally use GPT-4 to generate items capturing a set of targeted response types in observed challenge areas for refusal classification. We conduct error analysis on a classifier trained on an early prototype of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span>, and identify several categories of nuanced responses that the classifier mislabels. The majority of these categories are compliances containing caveats, warnings, etc. We then construct one-shot prompts for GPT-4 to generate synthetic responses with similar properties to enhance coverage of complex responses.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
              Most items take user prompts by XSTest category from the vanilla benign prompt set, while for a few categories the user prompts were also synthetically generated. See Appendix <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Complex Response Generation ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a> for all categories and prompts.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>Filtering, Auditing, and Sampling</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further filter responses created through open LMs by
assigning labels for each of our three target tasks using GPT-4 and recategorizing items that fail to match intended labels. We then audit the quality of these GPT-4 labels by sampling 500 items
and collecting human annotations as in §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 WildGuardTest: A High-Quality Human-Annotated Test Moderation Dataset ‣ 3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. This audit confirms the high quality of the GPT-4 labels, which agree with voted annotator labels on 92%, 82%, and 95% of items for prompt harm, response harm, and refusal labels, respectively. After our filtering and audit, we sample from these sets the following numbers of prompts along with matched refusal and compliance responses:
6,062 vanilla harmful prompts, 2,931 vanilla benign prompts, 4,489 adversarial harmful prompts, and 4,339 adversarial benign prompts, for 35,642 prompt+response items. We also include prompt-only items of 10,451 vanilla harmful prompts, 3,086 vanilla benign prompts, 11,289 adversarial harmful prompts, and 11,411 adversarial benign prompts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We sample from our other data sources (on which filtering/audit is not needed) as follows: from complex response, 1,167 each of refusal, compliance, and prompt-only items; from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span> data, 944 harmful prompts and 944 benign prompts; and from annotator-written data, 7,361 benign and 2,130 harmful prompts.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
                
                
                
              See Appendix <a href="#A3.SS7" title="C.7 Public Annotator-written Data ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.7</span></a> for further breakdowns.</span></span></span>
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span> and annotator-written items contain only prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span><span id="S3.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span>: A High-Quality Human-Annotated Test Moderation Dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTest</span> (<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>) to address the limitations of existing moderation tool evaluations discussed in §<a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, including harm classification on adversarial inputs and refusal detection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To construct <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>, we start with a test split of 1,725 prompt-response pairs from the synthetic vanilla and adversarial data as described in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 WildGuardTrain: Multi-task Moderation Training Dataset ‣ 3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.
We then collect annotations from three independent annotators for each prompt-response pair on prompt harmfulness, response refusal, and response harmfulness.
Fleiss Kappa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> scores are 0.55, 0.72, and 0.50 for the three tasks, indicating moderate to substantial agreement.
We apply majority voting to obtain gold labels, removing items that fail to reach at least two-way agreement.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            Lack of agreement is possible because we include an “unsure” answer choice.</span></span></span>
Finally, we run a prompted GPT-4 classifier on the dataset and manually inspect items on which the output mismatches the chosen annotator label, to further audit the ground-truth labels. See Table <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ C.6 Fine-grained Risk Taxonomy of WildGuardMix ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Complex Response Generation ‣ Appendix C More Details about WildGuardMix ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a> for the <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> label breakdowns and harm category splits according to our risk taxonomy, and Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Annotation Details ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> for more annotation details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp<span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">: XSTest with responses.</span></span>
We also create <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span> by extending XSTest with model responses to directly evaluate moderator accuracy for scoring models on a real safety benchmark.
We use the same LLM suite employed above for response generation to create completions for the prompts in XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, randomly sample from these outputs, and then collect human annotations similarly to <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> for response harm and refusal labels.
After filtering for inter-annotator agreement, we have a total of 446 prompts for response harmfulness (368 harmful responses, 78 benign responses) and 449 prompts for refusal detection (178 refusals, 271 compliances).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Training <span id="S3.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> with <span id="S3.SS3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span>, we instruction-tune <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> using <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mistral-7b-v0.3</span>
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> as a base model.<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
            We experiment with various base models (see Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1" title="H.1 Base Model Comparison for WildGuard ‣ Appendix H Extended Results ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1</span></a> for comparisons).
<span id="footnote7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mistral-7b-v0.3</span> shows top performance, but difference margins are small, emphasizing primary importance of <span id="footnote7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardTrain</span>.</span></span></span> We design a unified input and output format to capture the three tasks, providing the user prompt and model response as inputs, and training the model to output elements corresponding to all three tasks.
See more training details in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D WildGuard Training Details ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluating <span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools</h2>

<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> substantially improves performance relative to existing LLM safety moderation tools on all of the <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prompt harm</span>, <span id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">response harm</span>, and <span id="S4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">refusal detection</span> tasks, across existing benchmarks and our newly introduced <span id="S4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> evaluation sets.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Evaluation Setups</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation benchmarks.</span>
We test <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> and relevant baselines on ten publicly-available safety benchmarks, as well as our <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> across all three tasks. For public benchmarks on prompt harmfulness, we use ToxicChat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, OpenAI Moderation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, AegisSafetyTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, SimpleSafetyTests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, and HarmBenchPrompt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. For public benchmarks on response harmfulness, we use HarmBenchResponse <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, SafeRLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, BeaverTails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>,
and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span> <span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
              
              
              
            We count <span id="footnote8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span> among public benchmarks because the prompts originate from XSTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>.
The only evaluation for refusal detection other than <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> is <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span>, which we discuss in §<a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Table <a href="#A5.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix E Public Benchmarks for Evaluations ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Public Benchmarks for Evaluations ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> shows statistics of each benchmark. We report F1 scores for all evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Existing Safety Moderation Models.</span>

As in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
we test four LM-based moderation tools trained for prompt and response harmfulness detection: Llama-Guard, Llama-Guard2, Aegis-Guard-Defensive and Aegis-Guard-Permissive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
We test five additional models for response harmfulness classification: BeaverDam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, LibrAI-LongFormer-harm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>,
MD-Judge-v0.1
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, and two Harmbench classifiers from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al. [25]</a></cite> (HarmBench-Llama, HarmBench-Mistral). For refusal detection, we test LibrAI-LongFormer-ref <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. See Appendix §<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Details about Existing Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for additional model details. For closed tools, as in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we test the OpenAI Moderation API and GPT-4.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Results: <span id="S4.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> sets a new multi-task state-of-the-art</h3>

<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S4.T4.10.16.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.10.16.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">88.6</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> performs best for prompt classification.</span></span>
Results are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Results: WildGuard sets a new multi-task state-of-the-art ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. On both evaluation sets, none of the open baselines outperform GPT-4. However, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms GPT-4 by 1.8% average F1 on public prompt harmfulness benchmarks, and on <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> by 1.1%. Particularly on the <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">adversarial</span> subset of prompts, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> demonstrates a large improvement of 11.0% over the best open baseline and outperforms GPT-4 by 3.9%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> matches baselines on response harmfulness.</span></span>
Results are also shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Results: WildGuard sets a new multi-task state-of-the-art ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. For response harmfulness, on public benchmarks we see that <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms all open baselines by at least 1.8%, and is again the only open model to outperform GPT-4 (on two out of four evaluations). On <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> performs within 3% of MD-Judge, the best open baseline, with <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> performing better on responses to adversarial prompts by 1%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> substantially upgrades refusal detection.</span></span>
On full refusal evaluation, Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Results: WildGuard sets a new multi-task state-of-the-art ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that
<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms LibrAI-LongFormer-ref—the only existing open model that explicitly classifies refusal—by 26.4%, and the strongest open baseline by 21.2%. <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> also closes the gap between open models and GPT-4, with a score within 4.1% of GPT-4.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As in §<a href="#S2" title="2 The Status Quo of Safety Moderation Tools for LLMs ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
for the benefit of baseline models trained to detect response harmfulness rather than refusal, we also include refusal evaluation on a setting with harmful prompts only (<span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Harm.</span>).
In that setting, we see that <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms all open baselines, beating the best open baseline by almost 5%, and outperforming MD-Judge—the strongest model on response harmfulness—by a margin of 9.7%. Additionally, in this setting <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> outperforms the GPT-4 judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary.</span> Across all three tasks on previous benchmarks and <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> shows performance beating or on par with GPT-4, and substantially outperforming existing open models, with the single exception of MD-Judge on <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> response harmfulness, for which <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> is of the same caliber. This underscores the flexibility and practicality of <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, as it can be applied simultaneously to all three tasks of prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness, and response refusal classification with superior accuracy. Notably, <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> excels in refusal classification with benign prompts, a capability that no previous open model supports with adequate performance.</p>
</div>
</section>

</table>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 WildGuard Ablation Results ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows a series of ablations on <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span>,
as well as ablations on the multi-task setting comparing against single-task models for each task on the same training data (see Table <a href="#A4.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix D WildGuard Training Details ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and <a href="#A4.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix D WildGuard Training Details ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> for formats). We compare scores on <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> for all tasks, the average F1 of public evaluations (see <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>) for prompt and response harmfulness, and <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span> for response refusal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Each major component of <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span> helps to improve moderation performance.</span>
<span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span> is composed of four sources of harmful and benign prompts (See §<a href="#S3" title="3 Building WildGuardMix and WildGuard ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>); Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 WildGuard Ablation Results ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows that each is essential for high performance across tasks. For instance, when removing adversarial data, scores on almost all test evaluations drop, with a decrease of over 8.4 F1 points on <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> adversarial prompts. On the other hand, if we exclude the synthetic vanilla component, both public prompt harm evaluations and <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> refusal detection drop by 2.5-3.7 F1 points. Without <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span> data, performance drops on public evaluations across tasks, especially an F1 drop of 10.3 points on ToxicChat—which consists of prompts from in-the-wild human-LLM interactions.
Finally, excluding existing annotator-written data is much worse on public prompt and response harmfulness tasks (loss of 1.3-6 F1) and performs worse on all tasks in <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-task training improves the model performance.</span>
We additionally compare <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> trained under the multi-task setting to models trained on individual tasks.
On all tasks except refusal detection on <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSTest-Resp</span>, the multi-task model outperforms single-task models, demonstrating that multi-task training makes <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> an efficient unified tool without individual task performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Demonstrating <span id="S4.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> as a Moderator in Human-LLM Interactions</h3>

<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:41%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>ASR and RTA on <span id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildJailbreak</span> eval set with classifier models filtering out harmful prompts and responses.
</figcaption>

<tr id="S4.T6.4.4" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S4.T6.4.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T6.4.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.7</span>/<span id="S4.T6.4.4.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">1.7</span></td>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As a practical demonstration, we test <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> and other tools in a simulated chat moderation use-case in tandem with a completion model, detecting harmful prompts and responses and inserting benign refusals in place of the model’s original response when harm is detected.
For test prompts we use the full <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildJailbreak</span> (<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WJ</span>) validation set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, consisting of 2000 harmful and 250 benign adversarial prompts. We apply the moderation filters to Tulu-2-dpo-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, comparing against a baseline of Tulu-2 safety-tuned on the <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WJ</span> train set (Tulu-2 + <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">WJ</span>).
We measure Attack Success Rate (ASR) for harmful prompts and Refusal To Answer (RTA) rate for benign prompts, using GPT-4 to label responses for compliance versus refusal for both tasks. When using <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, Llama-Guard, and Aegis-Guard as moderators, we use prompt harmfulness and response harmfulness outputs for prompt and response components, respectively, while for MD-Judge we use response harmfulness output for the combined prompt and response input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4 Demonstrating WildGuard as a Moderator in Human-LLM Interactions ‣ 4 Evaluating WildGuard Against Existing LLM Safety Moderation Tools ‣ WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> yields the strongest performance both for refusing harmful jailbreak prompts and for avoiding over-refusal—for each model, it achieves lowest ASR while minimally increasing refusals to benign prompts.
Specifically, we see that Tulu-2 combined with <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> filter shows significant improvement on ASR (79.8% to 2.4%) with minimal sacrifice on RTA (0.0% to 0.4%). We also see that using <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> as a filter performs similarly to the directly safety-tuned Tulu-2 + <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WJ</span>. This shows that for use-cases where training is not feasible, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> can serve as a highly effective safety filter embedded in an LLM interface at inference time.
Additionally, even when using a safety-tuned model such as Tulu-2 + <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WJ</span>, we can further reduce ASR with a comparatively small increase in RTA by using <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> as an additional filter.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Works</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Safety Moderation Tools.</span>
There exists an extensive body of work on detecting hateful, toxic, offensive and abusive content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> on online social networking sites such as Twitter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and Reddit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.
With the recent state-of-the-art LMs (e.g., GPT-4, Gemini, Claude <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>) and their capabilities, researchers have begun using these models as judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> to assist in moderation.
Besides relying on frontier LMs,
recent studies have trained publicly-available open-source models such as Llama2-7b <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> on moderation data collected synthetically to cover a wide risk spectrum.
Some notable examples include Llama-Guard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, its follow-up Llama-Guard2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> (a version based on the Llama3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> model), Aegis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, MD-Judge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, the HarmBench classifier <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, and BeaverDam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.
Our work, however, differentiates itself in a few critical ways: <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> is trained to robustly handle adversarial inputs unlike many previous works, and is also multi-task across prompt/response harm as well as refusal detection, which no previous model supports satisfactorily.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safety Training &amp; Evaluation Datasets.</span>
Crucially, many previous works (e.g., Llama-Guard) do not release training data. Works that do release safety data include Anthropic’s red-teaming and RLHF work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, Aegis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, BeaverTails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> (only response harm), and SALAD-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> (only prompts)—but in contrast to <span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span> these are limited in coverage of adversarial model interactions and do not contain <span id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">In-the-Wild</span> prompts from real users.
Furthermore, the existing moderation evaluations
ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation, AegisSafetyTest, SimpleSafetyTests, Harmbench, SafeRLHF, and BeaverTails <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> have limited coverage over adversarial prompts (especially the benign adversarial category), cover a narrow scope of potential harms, or do not test for refusal detection and exaggerated safety behavior.
<span id="S5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span> fills this gap of high-quality human annotated evaluation data covering a broad spectrum of harm categories, jailbreaks, and all three important tasks of safety classification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, a unified multi-task open LLM safety moderation model capable of detecting diverse types of vanilla and adversarial harmful user prompts, harmful model responses, and model refusals. To support the development of <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span>, we create <span id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGMix</span>, which includes a comprehensive and varied set of training data (<span id="S6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTrain</span>) and evaluation data (<span id="S6.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>) for safety moderation tools. Through 10 public benchmarks and our newly introduced <span id="S6.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WGTest</span>, which specializes in more challenging adversarial prompts as well as refusals, we demonstrate the significant advantage of <span id="S6.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> compared to 10 existing open safety moderation toolkits.
Notably, <span id="S6.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> bridges the gap between open-source and closed-source safety moderation tools (e.g., GPT-4) by achieving performance on par with, if not better than, closed-source alternatives across all three classification tasks. With the public release of the <span id="S6.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuard</span> models and <span id="S6.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WildGuardMix</span> datasets, our research promotes the open and reliable future development of LLM safety moderation toolkits, paving the way toward safer LLM applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

this project.</p>
